I think the bigger issue is skipping the process through which you learn. Personally I learn the most when I am stuck on something for hours trying to figure it out and I miss all of that when AI gives a solution right away.

You get more done without realising you're learning less.

People have always been bad at critical thinking, it's a high level cognitive skill that requires practice.

Now that it can be outsourced,we will slowly lose this ability that we barely had.

This is my takeaway:

Authors analyzed ~300 workers doing ~1000 tasks. They collected self-reported measure of using critical thinking [yes/no], and estimate of cognitive effort of doing the task. Authors also measured workers' confidence in themselves doing the task or the AI doing the task.

They found: if someone is confident that AI can do the task, they report using critical thinking less, even though they think the task is easy. When someone is confident in doing the task and in evaluating AI responses, they use critical thinking more, even though they think the task is harder.

I think the paper is saying: low-domain expertise (read: confidence) + unrestricted AI tooling can eliminate the human from the loop. The fallout is better automation or unreliable systems. We need to resolve this ambiguity.

The question is: should low-domain expertise be coupled with more restricted AI tooling as a critical thinking forcing function? Are schools/workplaces right in restricting AI so students/new workers can reach the point of high domain expertise?

I'm either not seeing something or I do not see the point of this study.

Amount of "critical thinking" is basically amount of oversight, no? What's interesting is when the amount of oversight is inappropriate, leading to overconfidence in bad results (or, if too much oversight, lack of efficiency).

This paper does not seem to discuss results and correctness at all, ONLY the amount of critical thinking.

There's often a big gap between self perception and actual performance, I wonder if this actually tracks when measured.

Regardless, confidence in oneself is hardly measured, self report is likely as good as it gets.

"We surveyed 319 knowledge workers who use GenAI tools (e.g.,
ChatGPT, Copilot) at work at least once per week, to model how
they enact critical thinking when using GenAI tools, and how GenAI
affects their perceived effort of thinking critically. Analysing 936
real-world GenAI tool use examples our participants shared, we
find that knowledge workers engage in critical thinking primarily
to ensure the quality of their work, e.g. by verifying outputs against
external sources. Moreover, while GenAI can improve worker efficiency, it can inhibit critical engagement with work and can potentially lead to long-term overreliance on the tool and diminished skill
for independent problem-solving. Higher confidence in GenAI’s
ability to perform a task is related to less critical thinking effort.
When using GenAI tools, the effort invested in critical thinking
shifts from information gathering to information verification; from
problem-solving to AI response integration; and from task execution to task stewardship. Knowledge workers face new challenges
in critical thinking as they incorporate GenAI into their knowledge
workflows. To that end, our work suggests that GenAI tools need
to be designed to support knowledge workers’ critical thinking by
addressing their awareness, motivation, and ability barriers."
